article_title: The Impact of an LLM-Based Educational Agent on Learning Achievement, Cognitive Dynamics, and Student Perceptions in Computer Science Education
citation: Li, X., Liu, Z., Jiang, S., Chen, J., & Chen, W. (2026). The impact of an LLM-based educational agent on learning achievement, cognitive dynamics, and student perceptions in computer science education. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-026-00641-y
title: DBagent: an LLM-based educational agent combining RAG over a course knowledge base, external tool calling, memory, and ReAct reasoning
description: DBagent is a domain-specific educational agent built for an undergraduate database course on a university-wide educational AI infrastructure. It integrates a local course knowledge base via RAG, invokes external tools (search engine, image recognition, academic paper search, calculation, visualization), retains chat history in a memory module, and uses the ReAct reasoning pattern, which "enables LLMs to solve complex problems by alternating between logical reasoning and external execution". It uses Deepseek-r1-671b as base model and personalizes replies with the student's nickname.
requirements: A course-related knowledge base (courseware, teaching material, quizzes, handbook) converted to a unified data representation via an embedding model
Specialized training for students on interaction strategies such as Chain-of-thought prompting
constraints: Techniques for developing educational agents remain immature and their pedagogical efficacy is not yet well established, per the article's literature review
target_learners: sophomore computer-related majors in a database course
target_learning_goals: database knowledge and practical skills such as T-SQL programming and database design
examples: Used as a human-like tutor answering questions, clarifying concepts, and offering novel solutions during two practical sessions, replacing instructor-provided one-on-one help
key_sources: Li, X., Liu, Z., Jiang, S., Chen, J., & Chen, W. (2026). The impact of an LLM-based educational agent on learning achievement, cognitive dynamics, and student perceptions in computer science education. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-026-00641-y

article_title: Design-based research and technology-enhanced learning environments
citation: Wang, F., & Hannafin, M. J. (2005). Design-based research and technology-enhanced learning environments. ETR&D, 53, 5–23. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02504682
title: The article defines design-based research and identifies its characteristics
description: The article undertakes to define design-based research and identify its characteristics as a methodology for technology-enhanced learning environments. According to the abstract, the authors "define and identify characteristics of design-based research", establishing what counts as DBR and how it differs from other educational research approaches. This definitional work organizes the paper's subsequent treatment of DBR's importance, implementation principles, and challenges for TELE development.
requirements: The methodology must be defined and its characteristics identified before it can be applied to TELE research and design, as the article's stated purpose requires.
target_learners: Educational researchers and instructional designers working with technology-enhanced learning environments
target_learning_goals: Understanding and applying design-based research methodology in TELE research and design
key_sources: Wang, F., & Hannafin, M. J. (2005). Design-based research and technology-enhanced learning environments. ETR&D, 53, 5–23. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02504682

article_title: Measuring prevalence of other-oriented transactive contributions using an automated measure of speech style accommodation
citation: Gweon, G., Jain, M., McDonough, J., Raj, B., & Rosé, C. P. (2013). Measuring prevalence of other-oriented transactive contributions using an automated measure of speech style accommodation. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (2013).
title: Unsupervised Dynamic Bayesian Network model of speech style accommodation motivated by Speech Accommodation Theory
description: The model measures speech style accommodation from raw speech without labeled data or hand-crafted indexical features. It uses latent speaking-style states and binary accommodation states over conversational turns, with acoustic-prosodic observation vectors. As the article states, "Our model embodies two premises. First, a person's speech in any turn is a function of his/her speaking style in that turn, which is influenced by their speech style in their previous turn," and style also depends on accommodation to the partner. Parameters are learned with expectation maximization and inference uses the junction tree algorithm; the accommodation score is the fraction of adjacent turns where both partners' most likely style states match.
requirements: Speech recorded on separate channels per speaker, segmented into turns, with acoustic and prosodic features extracted per turn
constraints: The authors acknowledge that the link between theory and model structure could be further explored, and alternative model structures might perform better
target_learners: undergraduate students in face-to-face dyadic debate discussions
target_learning_goals: assessment of group knowledge integration processes, specifically other-oriented transactive contributions
examples: Trained on one set of 38 multi-segment conversations and tested on the other, using 70-dimensional normalized histogram observation vectors computed with the openSmile toolkit
key_sources: Gweon, G., Jain, M., McDonough, J., Raj, B., & Rosé, C. P. (2013). Measuring prevalence of other-oriented transactive contributions using an automated measure of speech style accommodation. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (2013). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-013-9172-5

article_title: CSCL towards the future: The second decade of ijCSCL
citation: Sten Ludvigsen. (2016). CSCL towards the future: The second decade of ijCSCL. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-016-9230-x
title: Use design-based research in CSCL to test new technological features and representations with clear scope and rigor
description: The editorial endorses design-based research as a methodological approach tightly related to CSCL. As printed: "In the CSCL field, DBR is an approach that makes it possible to test new technological features and representations (e.g., visualizations) with a clear scope and rigor (Jeong et al. 2014)." The editorial notes DBR principles have been altered toward use of both experimental and ethnographic methods, beyond the classical pre-posttest design with control groups in naturalistic settings.
requirements: Researchers must combine experimental and naturalistic settings, since the editorial states both are required to further explore key issues in the CSCL field
constraints: The editorial notes the classical DBR method was based on pre-posttest design with control groups in naturalistic settings, and principles have since been altered
target_learners: collaborative learners across CSCL research settings
target_learning_goals: testing and improving technology-supported collaborative learning designs
examples: The editorial cites Brown (1992) as the classical design-experiment approach and notes many CSCL researchers adopted DBR principles when it became accepted in the late 1990s
key_sources: Sten Ludvigsen. (2016). CSCL towards the future: The second decade of ijCSCL. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-016-9230-x

article_title: Modelling and Optimizing Mathematics Learning in Children
citation: Käser, T., Busetto, A.G., Solenthaler, B., Baschera, G.-M., Kohn, J., Kucian, K., von Aster, M., Gross, M. (2013). Modelling and Optimizing Mathematics Learning in Children. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0003-7
title: Dynamic Bayesian network student model of mathematical skills with prerequisite dependencies
description: The student model represents mathematical knowledge as a dynamic Bayesian network: "a directed acyclic graphical model representing different mathematical skills and their dependencies", where a connection means mastering one skill is a prerequisite for another. Skills cannot be observed directly, so the system infers them from task performance, updating posteriors after each solved task with the sum-product algorithm and a memory of the last five time steps. The net contains 100 skills ordered hierarchically by number range and difficulty, designed with experts' advice and inspired by knowledge space theory, allowing movements along all edges including backward movements to model forgetting and knowledge gaps.
requirements: Each skill is assigned to exactly one task, and the net structure was designed using experts' advice and incorporates domain knowledge
constraints: Posteriors are calculated over the last five time steps (memory of 5)
All probabilities are initialized to 0.5 in accordance with the principle of maximum entropy
target_learners: Elementary school children (grades 2–5) with developmental dyscalculia or difficulties in learning mathematics
target_learning_goals: Arithmetic operations and procedures (addition and subtraction)
key_sources: Käser, T., Busetto, A.G., Solenthaler, B., Baschera, G.-M., Kohn, J., Kucian, K., von Aster, M., Gross, M. (2013). Modelling and Optimizing Mathematics Learning in Children. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0003-7

article_title: Development and implementation of an IVR-based assessment system for student teachers’ professional vision
citation: Liu, T.-C., & Lin, Y.-C. (2025). Development and implementation of an IVR-based assessment system for student teachers' professional vision. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10463-4
title: Four-phase design-based research process for developing an IVR-based assessment system
description: The article organises the development of the IVR-based PVAS as a design-based research process combining scientific investigation with systematic solution development, emphasising iterative design, development, and evaluation with researcher–practitioner collaboration. The four phases are: (1) problem analysis and potential solution, (2) needs assessment and identification of design criteria via focus group interviews with an expert group, (3) design and construction of classroom events, assessment environment, and assessment task, and (4) evaluation and improvement with in-service teachers. The article states 'The development of the IVR-based PVAS included four phases,' and that the approach enabled continuous improvement and deep insight into student teachers' professional vision.
requirements: Collaboration between researchers and an expert group of practitioners (here: two IVR/e-assessment experts, three expert teachers, one classroom management specialist)
target_learning_goals: assessment of professional vision for classroom behaviour management
examples: Phase 2 used two two-hour focus group interviews yielding design criteria for the assessment environment, misbehaviour characteristics, and assessment task features; Phase 4's evaluation led to adding chair-rocking sounds and participant instructions
key_sources: Liu, T.-C., & Lin, Y.-C. (2025). Development and implementation of an IVR-based assessment system for student teachers' professional vision. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10463-4

article_title: Supporting motivation, task performance and retention in video tutorials for software training
citation: Hans van der Meij, Jan van der Meij, Tessa Voerman, Evert Duipmans. (2018). Supporting motivation, task performance and retention in video tutorials for software training. Education Tech Research Dev 66, 597–614. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-017-9560-z
title: Theoretical model combining demonstration-based training (DBT) and multimedia learning theory for video tutorial design
description: The model organizes video tutorial design around Bandura's four observational learning processes (attention, retention, production, motivation) and connects instructional features to them. Features include signaling, preview, pace, user control, practice, practice timing, practice files, anchoring in the task domain, conversational style, music, length, and the retention features segmentation, labels, simple-to-complex sequencing, pauses, and review. The article states the "instructional features in the model also connect to multimedia learning theory" with its "empirically tested principles for instructional design". All features except labels and music were incorporated in the study's tutorial.
requirements: Design features are tied to the four observational learning processes and should be selected according to which process they support
constraints: The model does not mention instructor-led support, since the prototypical context is an individual user working alone at a computer
Design features effective for novices may not work for more knowledgeable users due to the expertise reversal principle
target_learners: novice software users, e.g., upper elementary students
target_learning_goals: procedural software skills such as document formatting
examples: The study's tutorial taught six Microsoft Word formatting tasks with previews, demonstrations, and reviews, segmented into three chapters sequenced simple-to-complex, with videos capped at 3 minutes
key_sources: Hans van der Meij, Jan van der Meij, Tessa Voerman, Evert Duipmans. (2018). Supporting motivation, task performance and retention in video tutorials for software training. Education Tech Research Dev 66, 597–614. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-017-9560-z

article_title: Effects of Early Writing Intervention Delivered within a Data-Based Instruction Framework
citation: Pyung-Gang Jung, Kristen L. McMaster, and Robert C. delMas. (2017). Effects of Early Writing Intervention Delivered Within a Data-Based Instruction Framework. Exceptional Children, 83(3), 281–297. https://doi.org/10.1177/0014402916667586
title: Collect ongoing progress-monitoring data and use decision rules to individualize instruction for struggling writers
description: The article recommends that teachers implement DBI: establish baseline, set an ambitious long-term goal, monitor progress with CBM-W twice weekly, compare trend lines to goal lines, and make instructional changes when progress is insufficient. In the study, tutors made 47 instructional decisions, "averaging about two decisions per student," and the authors "strongly recommend that teachers collect ongoing progress-monitoring data and use those data to make instructional decisions based on students' responsiveness to intervention."
requirements: Reliable, brief progress measures (CBM-W) administered repeatedly
Trained implementers applying data-based decision rules and documenting changes
Ongoing support, such as weekly tutor meetings and check-ins, as provided in the study
constraints: Research-based intervention alone may not be sufficient for all students all of the time; about 90% of decisions were to increase a goal or change instruction
target_learners: Students in Grades 1 to 3 at risk for or identified with disabilities needing intensive writing intervention
target_learning_goals: Early writing transcription skills (handwriting and spelling) and writing performance
examples: Tutors implemented the eight DBI steps over 12 weeks, making 23 instructional changes (11 setting/format, 8 delivery, 4 content) documented on Changes in Instructional Plan forms
key_sources: Pyung-Gang Jung, Kristen L. McMaster, and Robert C. delMas. (2017). Effects of Early Writing Intervention Delivered Within a Data-Based Instruction Framework. Exceptional Children, 83(3), 281–297. https://doi.org/10.1177/0014402916667586

article_title: From classrooms to practice: does pre-service training for one health professions provide readiness for antimicrobial stewardship?
citation: Ade-Yusuf Oyinlola Rodhiat et al. (2026). From classrooms to practice: does pre-service training for one health professions provide readiness for antimicrobial stewardship? BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09843-y
title: Ducit Blue Foundation OH Pan-African AMR Internship/Mentorship Programme
description: The Ducit Blue Foundation programme targets early-career One Health professionals for AMR capacity building, combining structured learning with practical exposure. The article states the programme "strengthens young professionals' competencies in AMR, OH and leadership to tackle misuse, combining structured learning with practical exposure." Interns in the 2021–22 cohort, working with IFMSA, IPSF, IAAS, IVSA, NAMS and FAO, produced this study's curriculum analysis as their capstone projects. The authors describe such regional initiatives as essential for bridging gaps in pre-service AMR education in Africa.
requirements: Participation of interns from the target professions and collaboration with partner student federations and organisations
constraints: The study draws on universities selected through convenience sampling of participating interns, so coverage reflects programme participation rather than representative sampling
target_learners: early-career One Health professionals including medical, pharmacy and veterinary students and graduates in Africa
target_learning_goals: antimicrobial resistance governance, stewardship, policy analysis and evidence translation capacity
examples: The 2021–22 intern cohort's capstone projects formed the basis of this paper's curriculum mapping across nine universities in five countries
key_sources: Ade-Yusuf Oyinlola Rodhiat et al. (2026). From classrooms to practice: does pre-service training for one health professions provide readiness for antimicrobial stewardship? BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09843-y

article_title: Gendered achievement patterns in undergraduate education: evidence from a bachelor's program.
citation: Johansen M O, Lea K E, Eide H M K. (2026). Gendered achievement patterns in undergraduate education: evidence from a bachelor’s program. BMC Research Notes. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13104-026-07788-5
title: DBH public statistics portal with an openly released reproducible analysis workflow for describing grade distributions
description: The Database for Statistics on Higher Education (DBH) is Norway's central repository of administrative data on students, programs, and assessment outcomes, "publicly accessible via the DBH public statistics portal". The article extracts aggregated grade counts (year × sex × grade) for bachelor degrees in pedagogy at one large university over ten years, and states that "all the analysis code is openly available, enabling researchers to readily extend the approach to other programs, institutions, disciplines, or national datasets". It serves as a template for future descriptive investigations using administrative education data.
requirements: Aggregated grade-count data retrieved through the DBH portal for a specified study program and variables; the reproduction code repository for re-running the analysis
constraints: DBH suppresses or rounds very small counts in its public reporting, which may introduce minor imprecision in some grade categories
target_learning_goals: Describing and monitoring educational outcomes such as grade distributions across demographic groups
examples: The study's dataset consists of University of Bergen bachelor's program in pedagogy student statistics; code is available at the authors' repository and data at the DBH portal.
key_sources: Johansen M O, Lea K E, Eide H M K. (2026). Gendered achievement patterns in undergraduate education: evidence from a bachelor’s program. BMC Research Notes. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13104-026-07788-5

article_title: Defect-based scenario simulation teaching in the specialized skills training of nurse anesthetists: a before-after within-subject design.
citation: Ma Yanli, Li Han, Zhang Huan, Gao Fengli, Ma Xiaobei. (2026). Defect-based scenario simulation teaching in the specialized skills training of nurse anesthetists: a before–after within-subject design. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09098-7
title: Defect-Based Scenario Simulation: error-embedded high-fidelity simulation for specialized skills training
description: DBSS is an instructional method that uses simulation technology to create highly realistic, immersive clinical environments in which procedural flaws or latent risks are deliberately embedded. The article defines it as one where "the deliberate embedding of procedural flaws or latent risks within high-fidelity clinical simulations" compels learners to identify, analyze, and resolve problems. It aligns with Kolb's experience–reflection–conceptualization–application cycle and reflective learning theory, moving trainees from passive execution to active thinking. The article notes DBSS currently lacks an independent theoretical framework.
requirements: A scenario development team to design defect-based scripts grounded in standard operating procedures, real clinical cases and teaching goals
constraints: DBSS currently lacks an independent theoretical framework, per the article
target_learners: practicing nurse anesthetists with at least one year of anesthesia nursing experience
target_learning_goals: clinical judgment and risk prevention awareness
examples: Training delivered as lecture, defect-embedded video viewing, group defect identification, GAS-framework debriefing, and guided manikin practice over three weeks
key_sources: Ma Yanli, Li Han, Zhang Huan, Gao Fengli, Ma Xiaobei. (2026). Defect-based scenario simulation teaching in the specialized skills training of nurse anesthetists: a before–after within-subject design. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09098-7

article_title: Use of a Low-Cost Portable 3D Virtual Reality Gesture-Mediated Simulator for Training and Learning Basic Psychomotor Skills in Minimally Invasive Surgery: Development and Content Validity Study.
citation: Alvarez-Lopez F, Maina MF, Saigí-Rubió F. (2020). Use of a Low-Cost Portable 3D Virtual Reality Gesture-Mediated Simulator for Training and Learning Basic Psychomotor Skills in Minimally Invasive Surgery: Development and Content Validity Study. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/17491
title: Design-based research paradigm guiding iterative development toward a good enough prototype
description: The study adopts design-based research (DBR), described as "a process of using knowledge to design and create useful artefacts, and then using various rigorous methods to analyze why, or why not, a particular artefact is effective." Development proceeds through iterative cycles of abduction and deduction in which errors in design or function are detected and corrected—here via pilot testing by surgeons, engineers, and education experts—until a "good enough" functional prototype is obtained that can undergo validation studies. The article characterizes DBR as pragmatic, grounded in theory and real-world context, interactive, and iterative.
requirements: An interdisciplinary development team and iterative pilot testing with expert feedback to detect and correct design or function errors
constraints: Good enough prototypes are innovations that define ideas, practices, and technical capabilities rather than complete, finished systems
target_learning_goals: basic psychomotor skills in minimally invasive surgery
examples: Table 2 documents the iterative fixes: white forceps shafts, support devices for the fulcrum effect, a standardized mounting pad, a 45-degree LMC angle, and circular replacing quadrangular shapes in the virtual environment
key_sources: Alvarez-Lopez F, Maina MF, Saigí-Rubió F. (2020). Use of a Low-Cost Portable 3D Virtual Reality Gesture-Mediated Simulator for Training and Learning Basic Psychomotor Skills in Minimally Invasive Surgery: Development and Content Validity Study. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/17491
